questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Play text and what performance adds
questions.learningObjective: name what a performance supplies that the printed page cannot
questions.stem: A play's printed text fixes its words and its stage directions, and it cannot fix a voice, a pause, or a body. Which of these is something a performance supplies and the page cannot?

options.text: The duration and physical size of a moment in the room, since a page reports that a character speaks but not how long the silence before the speech is held
The causal order of the plot, since a production can rearrange scenes and so decide for itself what causes what among them
options.misconception: credits the production with a causal order the text already fixes, so mistaking revision for plotting

options.text: Whether a character counts as alive, since a performed body makes existence visible in a way a printed speech never manages to do
options.misconception: treats existence as something only a body can supply, when a direction can report presence with no stage at all

options.text: The play's meaning, since performers interpret the words and so settle finally what the text comes to be about
options.misconception: makes meaning a property of the performance alone, which leaves the words with nothing whatever to say

questions.explanation: The page and the stage carry different information, and the useful question is which is which. Printed text fixes words and instructions, so a reader meets a speech but meets it at whatever speed they read and with no sense of how large a pause preceded it. A performance fixes time and scale, and a held silence is a real duration that costs a minute of the evening whether the text marks it or not. The second option hands the production something it does not have, since a production may rearrange scenes but the causal order belongs to the plot, and cutting a scene is not the same as deciding what caused what. The third is wrong because a stage direction can report a figure's presence in a room with no stage built anywhere, so existence is already in the text. The fourth removes the words from the transaction, and a performance that means something else is a failure of performance rather than a fresh meaning.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader of the page gets that a reader in the row behind does not.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Dialogue and monologue
questions.learningObjective: say what dialogue supplies that a monologue to an empty room does not
questions.stem: In a dialogue, each line answers or deflects something just said. What does that pressure give a scene that a speech to nobody in particular does not?

options.text: A limit on what may be said, since a speaker has to fit an answer to what was actually put to them and cannot simply set out a case
Private access to a speaker's thinking, since speaking aloud to nobody lets a text report a mind without any interruption
options.misconception: credits the private speech with what the dialogue denies, so reversing the two devices entirely

options.text: A measurable pace, since two speakers cannot leave a gap as long as one can without the gap reading as a deliberate event
options.misconception: promotes a timing effect into the function of dialogue, when a pause is available to one speaker too

options.text: A wider spread of registers, since several voices let a text hold a comic tone and a grave one inside the same scene
options.misconception: credits dialogue with tonal range, when a register shift is a matter of situation and not of head count

questions.explanation: What a dialogue gives a text is constraint, and constraint is what generates action. A speaker in a scene has just been handed something, and the speech has to meet it, so the second line of an exchange is already a reply and already a choice among the available replies. That is why dialogue is the natural medium for conflict: nobody in a scene can simply set out a case and be done. The second option has the devices the wrong way round, since access to a mind without an interlocutor is exactly what the soliloquy provides and the scene denies. The third is a real effect of a pause and it is available to any speech, so calling it dialogue's function confuses a technique with a structural condition. The fourth describes something several characters can certainly do, and one character can hold two registers in a single speech, so nothing about the number of voices makes it the advantage.
questions.hint: Ask what a speaker is obliged to do that a speaker to nobody is not.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Soliloquy and private report
questions.learningObjective: state what a soliloquy can report that dialogue cannot
questions.stem: A soliloquy is speech a character makes on stage while alone or unheard. Which of these is something that arrangement can report and a dialogue cannot?

options.text: A character's reasoning while it is still unfinished, including a wrong turn that the character then abandons in the same breath
A character's settled intention, since a private speech is the one place a text may state an aim without anyone contesting it
options.misconception: treats an uncontested statement as the device's power, when a character in dialogue can state an aim and be argued with

options.text: A fact about what happened before the play, since a private speech can supply background no other figure has to know
options.misconception: credits a soliloquy with supplying background, which is the prologue's office and needs no stage presence

options.text: A reading of the play's own title, since a character talking to nobody can be direct about what everything is
options.misconception: makes a private speech an authorial verdict, where a soliloquy stays answerable as a character's own

questions.explanation: The soliloquy works because nobody is listening, and an unheard speaker has no one to persuade, so the text is free to let him think rather than report a finished position. That is what the option about a wrong turn describes: a person reasoning aloud starts somewhere, takes a false step, sees it, and goes another way, and that sequence is only available where the audience is being let into the process rather than handed a result. The second option describes something a character can say in a scene perfectly well, and being contradicted is not a limitation on what a play can report, it is the ordinary condition of the form. The third is the prologue's job. The fourth treats a character's private speech as the author's mouthpiece, and a soliloquy that announces the play's meaning only invites the audience to notice how far the speaker is from what the play is showing.
questions.hint: Ask whether the audience hears a result or a process.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Aside and its double audience
questions.learningObjective: say what an actor must supply for an aside to register
questions.stem: A character delivers an aside: speech the other characters do not hear, meant for the audience. What must an actor supply for the device to work at all?

options.text: A deliberate change of address, so the audience can tell at once that the line has left the scene's world entirely
Full consistency with the expression already on the face, so the aside reads as a thought and not as a second character
options.misconception: makes a wink the requirement, when a straight aside with a shift of address is the harder and plainer effect

options.text: A slower tempo than the surrounding dialogue, since an aside has to be carried over the noise a house makes
options.misconception: solves a problem of audibility with pace, when what the audience needs to know is who is being addressed

options.text: A turn of the head toward another character, since the convention works only when the audience watches who is excluded
options.misconception: makes the excluded figure the marker, where a glance at a character would give the line to that character instead

questions.explanation: The audience cannot hear the difference between a character speaking to a person and a character speaking to the house, because in both cases sound comes from the same mouth in the same direction. What the actor has to manufacture is the fact of a change of address, and it can be done with the eyes, the stance, a step to the front, or a shift of register, and a good production will often choose the least obvious of these. The second option describes the convention's failure mode, since a stage wink tells the audience exactly what the device exists to withhold from the scene's own world. The third is a real practical concern and has nothing to do with the device, because any line in a play has to be heard. The fourth has the wrong target: a glance at another character in the scene would make the line that character's business, and the exclusion the audience is enjoying is the exclusion of everybody standing on the stage.
questions.hint: Ask how the audience is told which world the line belongs to.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Stage direction as instruction
questions.learningObjective: distinguish what a stage direction does that no line of dialogue can
questions.stem: A stage direction is a sentence in a play that says what is not spoken aloud. Which function belongs to it and cannot be performed by any line of dialogue?

options.text: Reporting a condition no character on stage knows, such as weather, the hour, or a state of a room the plot will need
Announcing what a character is for, since a direction can state the purpose a given speech is being made to serve
options.misconception: credits a direction with interior access, when a purpose in a play must be spoken or shown by somebody

options.text: Introducing a figure and naming them, since a direction is the ordinary place a text records who is present
options.misconception: makes naming the direction's only job, when a speech can name a person and usually must

options.text: Fixing the wording of what a character says, since a direction is where a text records the exact words actually used
options.misconception: believes a direction can carry dialogue, which is the one thing it is written in place of

questions.explanation: Everything onstage is available to somebody's senses, so a fact the plot needs has to reach the audience by a route that does not pass through a character. A direction is that route. A storm can be described coming up from the low fields before anybody has noticed it, a room can be reported as cold or dark or already searched, and none of that can be spoken by a character who does not know it yet, because a character who knows it can only be made to volunteer the fact at the cost of the scene's tension. The second option asks a direction to do what only a speaker can do. The third is a job a direction sometimes does and certainly does not own. The fourth inverts the arrangement entirely, since a direction is what stands in place of the speech, and a printed acting text prints the speech itself.
questions.hint: Ask what a character would have to know in order to say this out loud.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A subplot's pressure on the main plot
questions.learningObjective: identify the effect that shows a subplot is doing work
questions.stem: A subplot runs beside a play's main action and shares at least one figure with it. Which effect on the main action shows that the subplot is working rather than merely present?

options.text: It changes what the shared figure can choose, so a decision in the main action is made under pressure the subplot supplies
It gives the play more room, since two strands of action offer more scenes to fill than one strand ever can use
options.misconception: counts the subplot's length, which is a symptom of an extra strand and not proof it connects

options.text: It supplies a foil, since a second figure with a different aim will always read as a contrast to the first one
options.misconception: treats contrast as proof of connection, since a foil can sit in a strand that changes nothing in the main action

options.text: It steadies the tone, since a lighter strand can relieve a grave one and keep an audience from growing tired of it
options.misconception: credits a subplot with balancing effect, which is a use it can have but not a sign it is joined to anything

questions.explanation: A subplot earns its place by touching the main action at a joint, and the joint is usually a person. What the second strand supplies is a second obligation or a second loss, and once a figure holds both, the options open to that figure in the main action have narrowed. That is checkable: you can ask what the character would have done in the main plot if the subplot had never happened, and if the answer is the same, the subplot is decoration. The second option is a measurement rather than a function, and it would justify adding any number of scenes. The third confuses a device a subplot may happen to supply with the connection that makes it structural, and a foil works by contrast rather than by pressure. The fourth is a real benefit and a poor test, because tone can be balanced by one comic scene or by a change of music.
questions.hint: Ask what the main action would look like if the second strand had never happened.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Reversal and its preparation
questions.learningObjective: state what must be established before a reversal can work
questions.stem: A reversal turns a situation into its opposite, so a servant becomes master or an accusation becomes a defence. What must the text have done earlier for such a turn to work?

options.text: Established the first reading in a form the audience can hold on to, so the reversal is a turn from something already seen
Withheld the cause of the reversal until the moment it operates, so the audience is surprised and the plot is not contradicted
options.misconception: makes concealment a requirement, when a reversal openly explained can be the stronger effect

options.text: Given the reversed figure a speech accounting for the change, so a transformation is accepted that would otherwise seem unearned
options.misconception: asks the play to justify the turn in words, where the text usually shows the turn and lets the argument follow

options.text: Held the reversal back to the last possible scene, since a turn placed late in a plot carries more weight than one placed early
options.misconception: turns a habit of positioning into a law, when a reversal early in a play can reorganise everything after it

questions.explanation: A reversal is a subtraction: it works by taking away a standing condition, so the condition has to be standing first. The audience must be able to say what the situation was, and be able to say it from something the text has actually established rather than from a vague impression, because a turn out of an impression is not legible as a turn. That is the condition the first option states, and it is the only one of the four that is necessary rather than merely available. Concealment is one way to make a reversal surprising, and an explained reversal is a common and legitimate choice, so the second option has turned a technique into a precondition. The third asks for a speech of justification at the exact point where the plot's force should be, and the fourth has made a preference into a rule.
questions.hint: Ask what the audience must already be able to say before the turn can register.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Recognition and the information gap
questions.learningObjective: identify the gap a recognition in plot depends on
questions.stem: Recognition in plot means a character learns who someone or something is. What has to be true of the play for that recognition to be dramatic rather than merely informative?

options.text: The character must have been acting on a wrong account of who the person is, so a belief is corrected and not just a label supplied
The audience must learn the identity in the same instant as the character, so the scene turns on a surprise that is shared
options.misconception: requires shared ignorance, where dramatic irony routinely depends on the audience knowing well beforehand

options.text: The identity must have been hidden from every other figure as well, so one discovery alone settles the question for good
options.misconception: demands universal ignorance, when a play may need several parties to learn a fact at different moments

options.text: The discovery must be put into words by the character, since a recognition left silent leaves the audience outside the moment
options.misconception: requires the recognition to be spoken, though a direction or a change of bearing can carry it to the house

questions.explanation: A recognition has force only where something is being corrected. If a character was mistaken about who stood in the room, the discovery reorganises the past as well as the present, and that reorganisation is the dramatic event; a character who held no prior account gains a fact and nothing more. So the condition is an error in the play, and the second half of the first option says what makes that more than a label. The second option is the standard misreading, and it is defeated by ordinary practice, since the commonest form puts the audience in possession of the truth several scenes before the character gets it. The third is an unnecessary condition, because a play can and does distribute a discovery unevenly among its figures. The fourth confuses what the audience must be able to follow with what a character must be able to say.
questions.hint: Ask what the character believed before, and whether the play made that belief.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Deus ex machina and the objection to it
questions.learningObjective: state the standard objection to a deus ex machina
questions.stem: A deus ex machina resolves a plot by bringing in something from outside it: a letter, an army, a long-lost heir. What is the standard objection to the device?

options.text: The rescue arrives unearned, so the ending is supplied by the machinery rather than by the causes the play itself built
The rescue disposes of the antagonist cheaply, so the conflict closes without the opposition ever having to be answered
options.misconception: takes the cheapness of the defeat as the objection, where the objection is to the plot's own chain of causes

options.text: The rescue cuts the play short, since a plot might otherwise have gone on for further scenes after the arrival
options.misconception: complains that the play ends when it ends, which is a requirement of endings and not a fault in a device

options.text: The rescue is not credible as fact, so a story should not rest on an event a sceptic would refuse to credit
options.misconception: demands factual credibility from a structural device, which is judged as plot rather than as report

questions.explanation: The objection is about who authored the ending. By the time the letter arrives, everything that decides the play has already been set in motion by characters and their choices, and the arrival then supplies a reason for a different outcome that none of those choices produced. The audience can see both accounts at once, the one it was following and the one now announced, and the second has no genealogy. That is what the first option names. The second identifies a real effect, since a deus ex machina does usually defeat an opposition cheaply, but cheapness is a symptom; the fault lies upstream, in a resolution that no cause inside the play supports. The third treats an ending as an interruption. The fourth asks the device to be true, and it is not a claim about the world that is in question but a claim about the structure of the plot.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything already in the plot could have produced that ending.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Tragic flaw as an explanation
questions.learningObjective: state a standard weakness in the tragic flaw device
questions.stem: A tragic flaw is a trait in a protagonist that a play treats as the cause of the fall. Which of these is a weakness in the device that criticism has always pointed at?

options.text: It puts the cause inside one person, so a play can account for a catastrophe without asking how the world around it made one possible
It makes the audience sympathise with the protagonist too early, so the fall arrives as a disappointment rather than as a shock
options.misconception: blames the device for the audience's sympathy, which a play manages with situation and a device cannot be blamed for

options.text: It depends on a fact the audience only learns late, so a reader who missed the flaw will not see the death as anything but accident
options.misconception: requires the flaw to be a late disclosure, though a trait stated in the first scene can carry a whole tragedy

options.text: It insists the flaw be a fault of character, so a play about bad luck or a wicked institution could not use the device at all
options.misconception: requires a moral vice, when a trait such as rashness or an appetite can be reported without being a sin

questions.explanation: The device is convenient in exactly the way a play about institutions cannot afford. Put a trait in the protagonist and the text has a cause ready-made, and it can then stage a catastrophe without showing a system that made one likely, because the explanation has been moved from the world to a person and the world escapes examination. That is the first option, and its second clause is the part that matters: the objection is not that the trait is untrue but that it is sufficient, and a sufficient personal cause lets a play leave structural causes untouched. The second confuses an effect on the audience with a fault in the mechanism. The third invents a requirement about timing that the device does not impose. The fourth insists on a moral reading of flaw and then draws an implausible conclusion from it, since a flaw can be an excess rather than a sin.
questions.hint: Ask what the device allows a play to leave unexamined.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Hamartia against structural cause
questions.learningObjective: contrast an error of judgement with a cause outside anybody's choice
questions.stem: When a play is said to have a hamartia, the error lies in a character's judgement. Which of these describes a cause that sits outside anybody's choice instead?

options.text: A debt that forecloses every option the play offers, so the collapse follows from the arrangement and not from any mistake in it
A rash choice by the protagonist, which remains an error in judgement even when its effects spread past the one who made it
options.misconception: gives the definition of the thing being distinguished from, and the wide reach of the effects does not move the cause

options.text: A family curse, which works on the plot's expectations and so accounts for the fall without needing a decision to explain it
options.misconception: calls a curse structural when it is a convention that removes the obligation to explain anything at all

options.text: A betrayal learned of too late, which is a limit on what a character could know rather than a fault in anyone acting
options.misconception: counts a timing accident as a structural cause, since whoever hears the news late still has to choose

questions.explanation: The two accounts of tragedy differ in where they put the pressure. A hamartia is a mistake, and a mistake is a thing a person does, which means the tragedy is reachable by a decision and somebody could have decided otherwise. An arrangement that forecloses the options makes a different claim: the situation is producing the outcome, and the play's evidence will be about the arrangement itself, its terms, and what it permits. The first option describes that, and the clause about the collapse following from the arrangement is what separates it. The second is the definition of the thing being contrasted and does not move when its effects spread. The third is a convention that short-circuits explanation rather than a structural cause that supplies one. The fourth changes a limit on information, which is real and important, but whoever gets the news late still chooses what to do about it.
questions.hint: Ask whether anybody could have chosen otherwise, and answer from the text.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Foil and what it reveals
questions.learningObjective: state what a foil character actually does for a play
questions.stem: A foil is a character defined by contrast with another. Which of these is what a well-built foil actually does for a play?

options.text: It makes one character legible by contrast, so a quality that would otherwise have to be stated can be shown in two lines of exchange
It supplies a second strand of action, so a play that must keep moving while the main plot rests has somewhere else to go
options.misconception: credits the foil with supplying a subplot, since a contrast can be carried by a figure with no plot of her own

options.text: It gives the audience relief, since a comic figure can break the strain of a grave scene without dissolving the play's seriousness
options.misconception: makes relief the foil's office, which belongs to a comic function and not to contrast at all

options.text: It puts the protagonist's choice to the test, so a rival who refuses the same offer shows plainly what accepting it cost
options.misconception: takes one possible use of a foil for its definition, since contrast works in ways other than a moral challenger

questions.explanation: A foil works by subtraction: the audience measures one figure against another and the measurement is the description. If one character is exact about money and the other calls a debt an arrangement, the second figure's vagueness is stated nowhere and does not have to be, because the first has supplied the measure. That economy is what the first option describes, and it is why foils are so often given small parts. The second confuses a figure with a strand of plot, and a foil may have no action beyond being present and answering. The third imports the comic function, which is a different job and often incompatible with the sustained contrast a foil needs. The fourth is a good example and not the definition, which is the trap, because the play would lose the device if every foil were a moral challenger.
questions.hint: Ask what a foil lets the audience measure without being told.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Stock character and the audience's work
questions.learningObjective: state what a stock type asks an audience to do
questions.stem: A stock character is one built from a familiar set: the disapproving parent, the shrewd servant, the boastful soldier. What does the convention ask an audience to do?

options.text: Recognise the type and anticipate its moves, so the pleasure is in watching a known shape behave the way it is known to behave
Judge whether the type suits this plot, since a convention is a starting point that the play still has to justify on its own
options.misconception: makes a convention answer to each plot, which is the demand a stock type exists precisely to spare the play

options.text: Supply the type's history, since a stock figure arrives already carrying a past the text would otherwise have to write
options.misconception: moves the audience's work onto a backstory, when the charge of a type is carried by the convention itself

options.text: Watch for the point where the type is broken, since a convention is worth using only if the play eventually refuses it
options.misconception: requires every convention to be subverted, when a type played straight is doing a job of its own

questions.explanation: A stock type is a contract the play makes with the audience in advance, and the audience's part of that contract is to have done the work already. They know the shrewd servant will advise, the boastful soldier will be shown up, the disapproving parent will refuse, and so the scene can be built on what will happen rather than on whether it will. That is why the type saves the playwright the work of establishing a person from nothing, and it is also why an audience can find the convention thin once the habit is old. The second option reverses the economy, since a stock type is precisely the place a play stops having to justify a person in advance. The third locates the audience's labour in supplying a past, which is not what the convention stores. The fourth turns a technique into a duty of subversion, and a type played straight is a legitimate and useful thing.
questions.hint: Ask what the audience arrives already knowing and therefore need not be told.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Pun as a dramatic instrument
questions.learningObjective: state what a pun does inside a scene
questions.stem: A pun puts two senses of a word or phrase into a single line. Which of these is something that lets a scene do what a plain statement cannot?

options.text: Let a character take one meaning aloud while the situation supplies the other, so that two readings are running at once
Save length, since one punny line can carry a paragraph of explanation and so spare the play an entire speech
options.misconception: makes the pun an economy device, when saving words is a side effect of the double reading it produces

options.text: Mark the turn of a scene, since wordplay conventionally arrives at the moment a serious moment gives way to a lighter one
options.misconception: ties the pun to a tonal function, which it can serve but which is not what the two senses are for

options.text: Fix a character's way of talking, since a fondness for wordplay marks a speaker as distinct from everyone else
options.misconception: credits the pun with characterisation alone, when what it mainly supplies is a second reading in one breath

questions.explanation: The pun's mechanism is simultaneity. A speaker takes a phrase in the sense the situation is using, the audience takes it in the sense the character is unaware of, and both are present in the one clause, so the line says two things while the character says one. That is what the first option describes, and it is why puns sit so well at the point where somebody is congratulating themselves. The second makes the pun a matter of tidiness, which is a real effect but not the device. The third assumes a fixed convention connecting wordplay to relief, and puns are at their sharpest in serious scenes. The fourth gives the pun the job of characterisation, which it can help with, and leaves out the two readings that are actually doing the work.
questions.hint: Ask what the audience hears that the speaker does not.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Prologue and delivered exposition
questions.learningObjective: state what placing exposition in an opening section lets a text do
questions.stem: A prologue delivers background before the play proper begins. Which of these is something that placing exposition in a separate opening lets a text do?

options.text: State a fact about a figure that the figure could not be trusted to report, since the frame stands outside the play's own evasions
Keep the play's action free of interruption, since a text can put its necessary facts in one place and then begin cleanly
options.misconception: credits the prologue with protecting the flow, when what it supplies is a report from outside the fiction

options.text: Give the audience a rule to judge the action by, since a law stated at the start makes the ending predictable in advance
options.misconception: converts a prologue into a statement of theme, which can be set down anywhere in the play

options.text: Set up a speaker whose authority the plot will overturn, so the opening frame is a position the reversal will take away
options.misconception: makes subversion a requirement, since a frame may simply hold for the length of a play without being overturned

questions.explanation: A prologue is the one place in a play where the text speaks with a standing the characters do not have. Nobody onstage can be trusted to deliver the frame, because a character reporting his own history is exactly what the play is in a position to doubt, but a voice outside the action can say what is so and still be right. That is the first option, and the clause about standing outside the evasions is the part that carries it. The second is a real benefit and not the reason the device exists, since a play with no prologue can equally keep its action clean and any interruption can be managed with a scene change. The third mistakes exposition for argument. The fourth is a common use of a frame, and treating it as a necessary structure is the error, because plenty of prologues simply establish and are never overturned.
questions.hint: Ask who could not be trusted to deliver the background, and why.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Chorus and its vantage point
questions.learningObjective: state the perspective a chorus supplies
questions.stem: A chorus speaks for a play as well as in it, and it speaks as a body of people rather than as one character. Which perspective does that arrangement give the text?

options.text: A position outside any single character's interest, so that a judgment offered is not offered by somebody with a stake in the outcome
A collective memory of what came before, so a chorus can report a history that none of the figures onstage shares
options.misconception: confuses a function the chorus may perform with the vantage point the device establishes

options.text: A nearer view of the action than any character holds, since a chorus is present throughout while the figures come and go
options.misconception: mistakes continuous presence for proximity, when what the chorus knows is bounded by the same stage

options.text: An authority over what will happen, since a chorus may state the outcome and so remove the ending from doubt

The third notices a repeated shape and infers a role from it, which is a claim about writing rather than about the chorus's standing in the action. The fourth describes a chorus turning its attention outward, which is a choice of subject and not a bar on acting; a chorus that comments can enter earlier and intervene in exactly the same terms.
questions.hint: Ask when the chorus arrives relative to the thing it might have stopped.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A chorus that cannot be trusted
questions.learningObjective: identify what makes a chorus an unreliable witness
questions.stem: A chorus in an invented play speaks four times: "The boy was found at the river with his shoes on and his coat buttoned." "They searched the bank for two days and the water never gave him up." "It was in the harvest month, and the miller was away that week." "Ask the miller." What in this speech makes the chorus an unreliable witness rather than a trusted one?

options.text: The last line sends the audience to an absent man, so the chorus ends by moving the blame rather than by reporting what it saw
The first line gives details about the body that no witness could hold, since a boy found in a river cannot report his own shoes
options.misconception: supposes the chorus is quoting the dead, where the line is a plain report of how a body was found

options.text: The third line volunteers that a man was away, so the chorus shows more knowledge of the week than a bystander could have
options.misconception: counts suspicious knowledge as the defect, when the chorus is a body of people and may have been asking

options.text: The chorus repeats the word water twice, so a repeated word is a sign that the speaker is working to persuade rather than report
options.misconception: reads a verbal habit as a sign of unreliability, which is a guess about style and not about the account

questions.explanation: A witness becomes unreliable at the point where the account stops describing and starts directing, and the fourth line is exactly that: it is not a report of the week but an instruction about whom to ask next, and it names a man who is not there to answer. The first three lines are the kind of thing a body of people could reasonably have gathered at a riverside, and the fourth turns the whole speech from a record into a direction, which is what an interested witness does. The second misreads the plainest line in the passage as an impossibility, since a chorus can describe a body it has examined. The third counts a fact as a fault, and knowing that the miller was away is what an investigating crowd would know. The fourth guesses from a word used twice, and style is not evidence about a speaker's relation to the truth.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four lines is not a report of anything.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A device claim the text contradicts
questions.learningObjective: find the detail that defeats a claim about a dramatic device
questions.stem: A critic writes of an invented play that it gives its protagonist no soliloquy, so the audience is kept strictly outside his reasoning. But the text runs: PRIOR alone. He sets down the glass, carefully, at the edge of the table where a servant would not see it. If I am to be a man who reasons, then I had better do it where nothing can be spilled on the reasoning. Which detail defeats the critic's claim?

options.text: The direction places PRIOR alone, so the speech is a soliloquy whatever the critic's inventory of the play says about it
The speech ends on the word reasoning, so a speech concerned with reasoning is a soliloquy by the critic's own test
options.misconception: grounds the counter-example in a keyword, when the staging is what contradicts the inventory

options.text: The critic used the word strictly, so a single speech of this kind is enough to show that the claim was overstated
options.misconception: wins the argument by a dispute over wording instead of by reading the direction the text supplies

options.text: The play is a tragedy, and a tragedy is said to require soliloquies, so the genre settles the question on its own
options.misconception: settles a local claim by genre convention, which is a rule of thumb and not evidence from this text

questions.explanation: A soliloquy is defined by who can hear the speech, and the direction answers that before the line does: PRIOR is alone, so nobody onstage is present for what he says. Once the direction has placed him, the claim that the play contains no soliloquy is simply wrong, and no amount of counting elsewhere will repair it. That is the first option, and the closing clause is the reason the inventory fails. The second finds a word that happens to be thematic and treats it as a form. The third is a dispute about a modifier and leaves the text unread, which is a losing move whatever the modifier means. The fourth reaches for a genre rule, and a genre expectation is a prior and not a reading of this direction.
questions.hint: Ask who is on stage when the speech is made.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a direction reports
questions.learningObjective: identify the clause of a direction that dialogue could not carry
questions.stem: An invented play opens: "A road at dusk. A storm coming up from the low fields, visible on the horizon before anyone speaks. A cart stands at the verge, its near wheel in a ditch, unattended. A woman comes to it, looks into the bed, and goes on without stopping. A man comes to it, looks into the bed, and stands there." Which clause does work no line of dialogue in the scene could do?

options.text: The storm coming up from the low fields, since the direction reports a condition in advance of anybody's knowledge of it
The woman going on without stopping, since a direction can record a choice not to speak that a speech could not report
options.misconception: denies a speech the power to report a silence, which a character can very plainly announce for herself

options.text: The wheel being in the ditch, since a direction can establish the state of a thing before any character has examined it
options.misconception: makes inspection by a character necessary, when a character who saw the wheel could describe it in a line

options.text: The two figures arriving and leaving, since a direction is the only place a text can record a character's presence at all
options.misconception: gives the direction a monopoly, since a character who enters may simply announce herself by name

questions.explanation: Everything else in that direction could be reported by somebody if the text were willing to spend a line on it. The woman could announce that she did not stop; either figure could mention the wheel; a character could come on and say who she is. The storm cannot be reported by anybody, because nobody in the scene has noticed it yet, and a direction is the only route by which it reaches the audience without being made into a conversation. That is the first option, and the clause about being visible before anyone speaks is the evidence. The second is a claim about speech that is easy to test and fails. The third requires a character to look, which the text has deliberately not arranged. The fourth claims a monopoly the direction does not hold.
questions.hint: Ask which fact no character in the scene is in a position to know.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A stage version and what it changes
questions.learningObjective: say what moving a line into a direction does
questions.stem: Two versions of an invented play survive. In the earlier version a scene opens on a kitchen table and a character says to the steward: "You have been eating in this house a month." In the acting version the same exchange is printed as a direction: "ORRIN, eating, does not look up. He has been eating in this house a month." What has the change from speech to direction done?

options.text: It puts the information where no character has to be its author, so an accusation reaches the audience without anybody making it aloud
It shortens the scene, since a direction can be delivered in less time than the line of dialogue it replaces
options.misconception: counts the saving, which is real but incidental and would not justify the change on its own

options.text: It gives the actor an instruction, so the printed text is now carrying directing work as well as the words themselves
options.misconception: reads the change as stagecraft instruction, when what has moved is the whereabouts of the information

options.text: It takes the line out of the play, so the acting version is a revision of the text rather than a record of a performance
options.misconception: concludes that a changed attribution is a rewrite, when the same words are still spoken by the same figure

questions.explanation: In the earlier version the accusation is somebody's, and its being spoken tells us who noticed and who chose to say so. In the acting version the words are still there and are still Orrin's to say, but the direction reports them about him to the house, so the audience receives an accusation and the character is not made its author. That is what the first option describes, and it is why the change is worth noting at all: the information has moved from a position inside the scene to a position outside it. The second measures the saving, which is a side effect. The third notices that a direction is read by performers and stops there, which describes the medium rather than the effect. The fourth concludes that a changed attribution is a changed text, and the same line is spoken in both versions.
questions.hint: Ask who is responsible for the words in each version.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Sound placed inside or outside the story
questions.learningObjective: classify sounds in a described scene by where they belong
questions.stem: A film scene is described as follows. Two men are in a kitchen at night. A fridge cycles on and off. Through a shut window a bus slows and goes. The man at the table looks toward the door and raises his voice: "Turn that down, would you." His wife calls from the next room that she cannot hear anything. A tune begins over their conversation, without source, and continues to the end of the scene. Which element in this description is non-diegetic?

options.text: The tune, since nothing in the scene accounts for it and it is laid over the conversation for the audience alone
The fridge, since a sound from an appliance is a convenience of the sound designer rather than part of the room
options.misconception: makes a source inside the world into an outside addition simply because it is unremarkable

options.text: The bus, since a sound arriving from outside a shut window is heard by the film and not by the two people inside
options.misconception: treats distance as exclusion, though a sound outside a window is still inside the story's world

options.text: The wife's denial that she can hear anything, since she is a figure reporting on her own senses rather than a sound in the room
options.misconception: confuses a character who talks about sound with a sound, and a speech is inside the world by definition

questions.explanation: Three of the four sounds have a place in the room or just outside it, and the description goes out of its way to establish that the characters respond to the noise around them. The tune is the one element nothing accounts for: it begins with no source, it is laid over the conversation, and neither the man at the table nor the woman reacts to it, so there is nobody in the story for whom it is audible. That is the first option, and its two clauses are the test applied twice. The second would make ordinary mechanical noise into an outside addition, which is the opposite of what the appliance is. The third reasons from distance rather than from whether the story contains the source. The fourth is a speech rather than a sound, and every speech in a film is inside its world.
questions.hint: Ask which sound the characters would have had to react to and did not.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A reversal made of a scene
questions.learningObjective: say what a reversal in a passage is built from
questions.stem: An invented scene runs: a clerk named WEIL is shown being dismissed, and he thanks the man who has dismissed him and asks when he should come back. The manager, embarrassed, says that the order came from above and that he himself never wanted it. A director's wife then enters with a ledger, having been sent for by the dismissed man before he left. What question does this scene raise, and how does it treat it?

options.text: How the dismissal came to be reversed, and the scene treats it as complete, since the wife's arrival supplies the authority the manager could only apologise for
No question at all, since the scene ends with the ledger and a ledger settles every matter it is opened upon
options.misconception: assumes a document resolves anything, which is the assumption the manager's apology has just contradicted

options.text: Whether the manager is telling the truth, and the scene answers it against him, since only a liar would say he never wanted the order
options.misconception: takes an unverified statement of feeling as decisive, when the scene's evidence is the arrival of the wife

options.text: Why the wife was sent for, and the scene leaves that open, since the text never says which of them asked and both were there
options.misconception: raises a question the text has already answered by naming who sent for whom before the man left

questions.explanation: The scene builds a reversal out of a substitution: the man who has the power to confirm the dismissal is a man who never issued it, and the authority that can settle the matter walks in afterwards. The question the scene raises is whether the dismissal can be undone, and the answer is delivered rather than withheld, because the wife's entrance is the text supplying the thing the manager could only apologise for. That is the first option, and the last clause is what makes it a resolution rather than a question left open. The second is defeated by the manager's own speech, which shows a document is not the same as an authority. The third treats a man's claim about his feelings as evidence and overlooks that the scene is built on a fact about who gave the order. The fourth raises a question the text has already closed.
questions.hint: Ask who has the standing to undo the order, and when that person arrives.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a soliloquy commits a character to
questions.learningObjective: say what a soliloquy exposes about its speaker
questions.stem: A soliloquy in an invented play runs: "I have told her the roof is sound. I have told her twice, and the second time I looked at the floor while I said it, which is the sort of thing a man does when he is asking to be contradicted. Nobody contradicted me. That is the part I cannot put down." What question does this speech raise, and how does it treat it?

options.text: Why the speaker wanted a contradiction and did not get one, and the speech treats it as answered by him, since he names the wish and the want
Whether the roof is in fact sound, and the speech treats it as open, since no one in it has been near the rafters
options.misconception: asks after the roof when the whole speech is about the speaker and what he wanted to be told

options.text: Whether the woman was complicit in the deception, and the speech treats it as proved, since her refusal to contradict is treated as agreement
options.misconception: reads a silence as collusion, when what the speech puts the weight on is the speaker's own disappointment

options.text: No question at all, since a soliloquy is by convention an aside about matters already settled in the plot
options.misconception: makes a soliloquy a formality, when this one ends on something the speaker plainly cannot account for

questions.explanation: The speech is about the speaker's own conduct, and the question it puts is why he wanted the other person to contradict him, which is a thing a speaker can recognise in himself without being able to explain it. The last line names the want and names it as a weight, so the question is raised and simultaneously held open by the figure who raises it, and the closure is on the observation rather than on an answer. That is the first option, and the fact that both halves are done by the speech is what distinguishes it. The second asks after the roof, which the speech mentions only as the occasion. The third builds a charge against the woman out of a silence. The fourth treats the soliloquy as decorative, and this one ends on an unaccountable thing.
questions.hint: Ask what the speaker wants from the other person and is disappointed not to get.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A pun doing argumentative work
questions.learningObjective: say what a pun is doing to the argument of a scene
questions.stem: In an invented play, a steward is clearing out a ruined house and tells the new owner: "The roof held. The roof has held for nineteen years, through two winters and a marriage, and it will hold for you as long as you keep meaning it to." What question does this speech raise, and how does it treat it?

options.text: What the roof is being made to mean, and the speech treats it as settled into a claim, since the phrase about meaning lets the steward claim credit for the house
Whether the roof is structurally sound, and the speech treats it as settled by the count of two winters, which is the only evidence offered
options.misconception: reads the argument as if it were an engineering report, ignoring the terms the speech is trading in

options.text: Who will pay for the repairs, and the speech leaves it open, since the new owner has not yet been told what anything costs
options.misconception: supplies a question the text never raises, and the speech is about a transfer rather than a price

options.text: No question at all, since a joke in a play closes a matter and lets the scene move on to the next business
options.misconception: assigns a comic job to the line, which is doing something more pointed than a joke

questions.explanation: The last phrase is a double reading, and both of its senses are in play at once: the roof lasts as long as the owner intends to keep it in repair, and the house has lasted as long as somebody meant it to. The first sense is practical and the second is a claim about ownership, and putting them in one clause lets the steward hand over a compliment and a condition in the same breath. The question the speech raises is what is being claimed, and it is treated as answered by the wording, which does the claiming on the speaker's behalf. That is the first option. The second takes the speech at its most literal and misses the phrase that is doing the work. The third raises a question about money that the text never poses. The fourth calls the line a joke, when it is a transfer of blame dressed as a gift.
questions.hint: Ask what the last clause says in both of its senses.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a prologue fixes before the play
questions.learningObjective: say what a prologue establishes and how it holds
questions.stem: An invented play opens with a prologue: "This house was built in one year by a man who had bought the timber, cut it himself, and sold the house before the roof went on. His name was not kept. His sons kept the quarrel, and the quarrel is the play. Everything you will be shown tonight was decided before the first of you were born, and none of it was decided by love." What question does the prologue raise, and how does it treat it?

options.text: What the quarrel is actually about, and the prologue treats it as settled in advance, since the last clause rules out the explanation the audience would prefer
Why the builder's name was not kept, and the prologue leaves it open, since it mentions the omission and then declines to explain it
options.misconception: sees an unstated cause as the play's question, when the prologue points elsewhere on purpose

options.text: Whether the roof was ever finished, and the prologue answers it against completion, since a roof begun late is the image of the family
options.misconception: reads a detail as a symbol on the play's account, when the prologue uses it as a fact about a transaction

options.text: No question at all, since a prologue exists to settle the ground so the audience can concentrate on what follows
options.misconception: makes the prologue a neutral clearing of the stage, ignoring the judgement in the last clause

questions.explanation: The prologue hands the audience a frame and then closes one door in it. It says the quarrel is the play, and it says the quarrel was settled before anybody in it was born, and the last clause takes love out of the explanations on offer before the audience has finished expecting it. The question the prologue raises is what the quarrel is about, and the last clause answers it by exclusion, which is a decision rather than a silence. That is the first option. The second finds an unstated fact and treats the prologue's silence about it as the play's question, and the silence is doing work rather than leaving a gap. The third finds a symbol where the text has a transaction. The fourth describes a prologue that takes no position, and this one takes a clear one in its final clause.
questions.hint: Ask what the last clause rules out before the audience can expect it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Where a comedy of manners aims
questions.learningObjective: identify the target of a comic scene and how the scene holds it up
questions.stem: A scene from an invented comedy runs. A young woman is offered a marriage by a suitor who explains, at length and with perfect courtesy, that her father's estate is entailed and that her mother has been unwell since the spring. A second suitor says nothing about estates and asks instead whether she plays the fiddle, and is confirmed as acceptable by everyone present. What question does the scene raise, and how does it treat it?

options.text: What counts as a serious offer, and the scene treats it as settled by contrast, since the second suitor's small question is preferred over the first's long account
Whether the fiddler suitor is sincere, and the scene leaves it open, since nobody has tested the second man and everybody has heard the first
options.misconception: suspends judgement on the one figure the scene never indicts, which is the whole point of the contrast

options.text: Why the estate is entailed, and the scene treats it as a practical difficulty the first suitor has honestly described
options.misconception: takes the suitor's account at face value, when the scene is built on what his courtesy is for

options.text: Whether the young woman consents to either match, and the scene decides it by the second suitor's question about the fiddle
options.misconception: reads a comic scene as supplying a marriage plot, which it uses rather than examines

questions.explanation: Both suitors are judged against the same code and they fail or pass it in opposite ways, and that is what the scene is for. The first suitor observes every rule of courtesy and applies them to a valuation, so the audience is not laughing at bad manners but at correct ones put to a use nobody wanted; the second suitor breaks the rules of address entirely and is preferred for it. The question the scene raises is what makes an offer serious, and it is answered by juxtaposition rather than by statement, which is why the text can answer it without a verdict. That is the first option. The second asks the scene to withhold judgement on a figure the scene is using, not examining. The third takes the first suitor's account at face value, which the structure forbids. The fourth imports a marriage plot the scene is using as a frame.
questions.hint: Ask what the two suitors do with the same set of rules.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The question a problem play refuses
questions.learningObjective: say what a problem play leaves unresolved and how the text leaves it
questions.stem: A play from an invented tradition ends like this. The last scene has a landowner who has cleared a common for grazing been met by villagers who have signed a paper asking for it back. He reads the paper, and asks whether they have a lawyer. They say they have not, and have not needed one until this year. He says that is the first sensible thing he has heard all day, and asks for the paper again, and reads it aloud to the company. The play then ends. What question does this ending raise, and how does it treat it?

options.text: Whether the common will be restored, and the ending treats it as undecided, since a man who has just been shown the strength of a paper is left holding it
Whether the landowner will apologise, and the ending treats it as settled by his second reading, which shows the paper has changed him
options.misconception: reads a changed tone as a completed conversion, when the text has stopped at the moment of the reading

options.text: Who wrote the paper, and the ending leaves it open, since the company has come together without any author being named
options.misconception: seeks a biographical fact the text has deliberately not supplied and the argument does not need

options.text: No question at all, since a play that has set out a social wrong should end by showing it put right
options.misconception: assumes a problem play is a problem solved, which is the definition it deliberately refuses

questions.explanation: The ending stops at the point where the landowner has accepted that the demand is serious and has not decided what to do about it, and the significance of that stop is the whole argument. Nothing in the last scene says the common will be restored, and the closing action is a man asking for a paper twice, which is a way of conceding the force of an argument without conceding its conclusion. The question the ending raises is the practical one, and the text treats it as undecided on purpose, having arranged for the decision to rest with a character who has been made to see what he was doing. That is the first option. The second mistakes a change of tone for a completed change of mind, and the text is careful to stop before any of the language of apology. The third asks after authorship, which is not what the paper is for in the scene. The fourth states the convention the form is defined against.
questions.hint: Ask what the last action commits the landowner to and what it leaves out.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A recognition in a scene
questions.learningObjective: say what a recognition in a scene corrects and what the audience already has
questions.stem: In an invented scene, a young man who has believed throughout that the woman speaking to him at an inn is his employer's sister reveals that she is his employer's wife. The scene has already shown a coach changing horses outside, a letter in her hand, and the innkeeper's daughter curtsying to her. What question does the scene raise, and how does it treat it?

options.text: What the young man has been getting wrong, and the scene treats it as fully answered, since his error has been visible in three details and he can now count them
Why she let him believe it, and the scene leaves that unexamined, since a recognition is about who somebody is and not about motive
options.misconception: treats an unexplored motive as the scene's central question, when the text has been arranging a misrecognition instead

options.text: Whether the audience was meant to see the three details, and the scene refuses to say, since a play does not comment on its own evidence
options.misconception: asks a question the staging has answered, since the details were put on stage before the reveal for the audience to use

options.text: Whether the employer knows, and the scene treats it as settled, since a wife on a coach must have told her husband where she was going
options.misconception: infers a fact about an absent character from a coach, which the text gives no reason to supply

questions.explanation: A misrecognition is a debt the scene pays, and the payment works because the debt was visible before the payment. The coach, the letter, and the curtsey are three pieces of evidence the young man had in front of him and did not combine, and the reveal does not introduce new information so much as rearrange what was already there, which is why a reader can go back over the scene and find it. The question raised is what he has been getting wrong, and the scene treats it as answered, because a recognition is complete when the character can re-read his own earlier evidence. That is the first option. The second makes a motive the subject, and the scene is organised around an identification rather than a decision. The third asks the text to report on its own evidence. The fourth supplies a fact about an absent man on the strength of a coach.
questions.hint: Ask what the audience was given to put together before the reveal.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Whether a fault explains a fall
questions.learningObjective: weigh a personal explanation against one the play's own evidence supports
questions.stem: An invented tragedy ends with a young man dead. The play has given him an appetite for the one thing his father's contract forbids, and he has been warned about it twice. It has also shown that the contract cannot be varied, that the one man who might have varied it sold his interest a year earlier for a sum nobody mentions twice, and that the daughter who loves him was given no copy of the terms. What question does the ending raise, and how does it treat it?

options.text: Whether the father's contract produced the death, and the ending treats it as genuinely open, since the play has supplied the appetite and the arrangement in equal measure
Whether the young man's appetite explains the death, and the ending treats it as answered against him, since the warnings make his choice a knowing one
options.misconception: settles a two-cause argument on the strength of a warning, when the play has built the second cause at equal height

options.text: Why the daughter's terms were withheld from her, and the ending treats it as settled, since a person not told a rule is not bound by it
options.misconception: draws a legal conclusion from a staging fact, which is a rule the play has not invoked anywhere

options.text: What the sum was paid for, and the ending refuses the question, since a figure omitted twice is a figure the audience should notice
options.misconception: turns a deliberate omission into a refusal, when the text has simply declined to repeat a number

questions.explanation: The play builds two causes and refuses to rank them, and the ending inherits that refusal. The appetite is real and the warnings make it a knowing one; the contract is equally real and the play has spent scenes showing that it could not be varied, that the man who might have varied it had already sold out, and that the daughter most affected was never shown the terms. Nothing in the last scene adjudicates between them, and the fact that the audience is left holding both is the argument the ending makes about how such deaths happen. That is the first option, and the phrase about equal measure is the evidence. The second decides the case on a warning, and a warning is one of the two things the play has supplied. The third imports a legal rule the play never states. The fourth mistakes an omission for a withholding.
questions.hint: Ask how much stage time the play gave each of the two causes.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a production claims and what it keeps
questions.learningObjective: weigh two accounts of what a performance adds to a text
questions.stem: Two accounts of the same play are set side by side. The first says a production interprets the text and therefore can mean something other than what it says. The second says a production fixes what the text can mean by deciding who is standing where and how long anyone waits. Which account better supports the claim that performance has a real effect on a play?

options.text: The second, since an interpretation is free but the decisions it is made of are not, and those decisions limit what any reading can claim
The first, since the freedom to interpret is what distinguishes a performed play from the page on which it waits
options.misconception: makes liberty the effect, when the claim is about constraints a production sets and cannot then ignore

options.text: The second, since waiting is the only decision a performance makes and every other choice is a matter of the text
options.misconception: narrows the effect to one decision, so a text held wrong cannot be argued from at all

options.text: Neither, since a performance is an illustration of a text and the only real question is whether it has been illustrated well
options.misconception: restores a decorative account of performance, which the two accounts on offer both reject

The clock is in shot, running, and the sound of it is the only sound for forty seconds. Then a hand, still, and nothing else." Which description better supports the claim that the screen version has changed what the scene is about?

The stage version, since it reports both figures' behaviour at once and the screen version can only look at one thing
options.misconception: supposes a camera can hold less than a stage, when framing and editing are both available to it

options.text: The screen version, since a low angle is a device for making a figure look powerful and that is what changes the subject
options.misconception: settles the question on a framing choice, ignoring the forty seconds the description spends on sound

options.text: Neither, since the two versions describe the same two people at the same table and the subject cannot have moved
options.misconception: insists the subject is fixed by the situation, when how long a clock is heard is a fact about the scene

The third rests on the low angle, which is a small choice compared with the sound. The fourth holds that the subject is fixed by the furniture, when a duration is part of what a scene contains.

Two accounts of this are offered: that the chorus is filling the intervals between the play's business, or that the chorus is supplying a view of the play's events that no figure inside them could take. Which better describes what the three entries do?

options.text: The second, since the three occasions are the three points at which the play's own characters are least able to comment on what has happened
The first, since none of the three entries touches the plot and each occupies a gap the play would otherwise have to bridge itself
options.misconception: judges a chorus by what it does to the plot, when a chorus that only mattered to the plot would be redundant

options.text: The second, since a chorus speaks for everyone and therefore can be held to represent a view the play is endorsing
options.misconception: assumes a chorus endorses, when its position is precisely that it has no stake and can be wrong

options.misconception: renames the device, since a narrator is outside the time and a chorus is standing in it

The second: a general believes a report that a rival has paid a judge; believing it, he moves his army; the movement is the fact the rival wanted. Which summary better meets the standard of a well-made plot?

The first, since a chain of accidents is harder to arrange than a chain of decisions and so shows more construction in the telling
options.misconception: praises difficulty of assembly, when the standard is about the causes being visible in the outcome

options.text: The first, since a war caused by one man's forgetfulness is a more serious warning than a war caused by a rival's payment
options.misconception: judges the plot by the weight of its subject rather than by the tightness of its causes

options.text: Neither, since both summaries leave out what the reader thinks of the people involved and so neither can be judged at all
options.misconception: makes an audience's reaction a condition of a plot's construction, which is a different question entirely

questions.stem: Two scenes from an invented play are described. The first is set entirely in unrhymed iambic pentameter and is a character explaining to a judge why a debt was not paid. The second is in plain speech and is a clerk reading an inventory of what was in a room. Which description better supports the claim that the play is using form to mark the weight of what is being said?

The second scene, since a list of objects gains its force from being unadorned and the play has saved its verse for other matters
options.misconception: assumes plain form is a mark of force, when the claim is about a form being spent where it costs most

options.text: The first scene, since a judge is a person of rank and the play has followed the convention of giving rank its metred speech
options.misconception: applies a rank convention the play may not be using, since the description gives no such rule anywhere

In the second, a scene is given to a lord forbidding his steward to speak to a young woman; the steward obeys, the young woman asks why, and the lord explains that the steward is to be married within the month. Which description better shows a reversal being prepared?

The second, since the explanation tells the audience exactly what the rule is for and a reversal with a stated cause is a prepared one

The third treats surprise as the measure, and a reversal can be fully prepared and entirely expected. The fourth requires the break to be shown, which is a condition on the plot's ending and not on the preparation of its turn.

the man taking the post, which cannot happen after the letter is hidden and before the rival writes
the rival writing in her name, which is only worth doing once the man is far enough away to be misled
the man resigning the post, which is the consequence of the letter he believes he has received
the woman finding the letter unread, which is the last thing the plot reports and settles nothing

The post is second, since a man must be at a distance for a forged letter to be worth writing. The forged letter is third, because the rival writes to a man who is away and not to one standing in the woman's company. The resignation is fourth, and it follows from the letter he believes he has received, so it cannot precede the forgery that prompted it. The discovery of the original, unread, is last, since it is the thing every earlier event has been keeping out of reach. Nothing in the sequence needs a further fact to justify its place, which is what the standard is asking for.

the cutting of scenes that will not fit inside that running time

the shooting of the replacement material once its length and content are settled

Running time is second, because it is a constraint on everything that follows and choosing it later would invalidate the decisions in between. The cutting is third, since the film cannot know what to replace until it knows what it is dropping, and the material is decided by what has been kept as much as by what has gone. The replacement is fourth, and it is the step where the adaptation actually becomes one rather than a shortening. The shooting is last, because a replacement that has not been decided cannot be filmed and a filmed replacement nobody has agreed on is unusable.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a tragic flaw leaves unexplained
questions.learningObjective: explain what a personal cause in a tragedy can and cannot account for
questions.stem: A play ends with a young heir dead because of a temper his household has indulged since he was a boy. The play has also shown that his father's will could not be altered and that the one lawyer who might have argued otherwise was dismissed years earlier for a fee. Explain what the personal cause in this ending accounts for and what it leaves untouched, and what a reader has who notices both.

answer.exemplar: The temper accounts for the shape of the last day and for nothing else. It tells the audience why a specific person, on a specific morning, could not stop himself, and it gives the catastrophe a character at the centre of it, which is a real and useful thing for a tragedy to have. What it cannot account for is the size of what he is frustrated about. A will that cannot be altered and a lawyer bought off years earlier are not produced by anybody's temper, and a reader who stops at the flaw has been given an explanation of a decision rather than of a situation. That is the limit the device imposes: it relocates the question from why the world was arranged this way to why one person could not bear it, and a play that only needs the second question has been served. A reader who notices both is in a different position, because the two explanations compete rather than cover for each other. The flaw says the catastrophe needed a particular man; the will and the fee say it was going to fall on somebody. The consequence for the reader is that neither account can be believed alone, so the question of responsibility stays open in a way that a single cause would have closed. The strong explanation will name what the temper explains, name the two facts the temper does not touch, and then say what the reader ends up holding. A weak answer will say only that the flaw is the cause and stop there, which is exactly the account the play's own evidence is built to prevent.

questions.explanation: An explanation of a device has to do three things and this kind of item fails when it does only the first. It must state what the device accounts for, since the temptation is to grant the flaw a total explanatory reach it cannot have and to let a tidy ending substitute for an account. It must name what the device leaves untouched, which is a matter of checking the play's other evidence rather than of general theory, since the will and the fee are on the stage and not in the critic's head. And it must say what a reader has who holds both, because the question asks for that and an answer that closes on a claim about the flaw rather than on the reader's position has not finished. The trap here is the completeness of the personal explanation, which feels like an answer precisely because it accounts for something real.
