questions.topic: Why a rescue from outside is criticised
questions.learningObjective: explain what a plot loses when it ends by arrival
questions.stem: A play in its last scene is saved by a regiment that arrives at the gate, and a rider sent for in the penultimate scene is the reason the play ends well. Explain why this ending is criticised, what a reader is able to compare because of it, and what an ending would have to do instead.

answer.exemplar: The criticism is not that the ending is lucky. It is that the ending has been authored by somebody outside the play. Every decision that matters in the last scene has been made by the rider and the colonel, and the characters whose choices built the story are in a position to be rescued rather than to resolve anything, so the question of what the earlier scenes were for has been answered by a letter arriving. A reader is left able to compare two accounts of the plot at once: the one in which a series of choices brought the characters to a gate at a particular time, and the one in which a coincidence of timing replaced the need for those choices. Those two accounts cannot both be the plot, and the reader has to discard one, which is the loss. A reader who notices this is in a different position from one who simply feels relieved, because relief requires the ending to be taken on its own terms and the comparison does not permit that. An ending that works has to be made out of what the play has already established: the person who is sent for must be answerable for something that grew out of the earlier action, the decision to send must be costly to somebody, and the arrival must settle a question the play has been asking rather than introduce a solution nobody in the story had a stake in. The strong explanation will name who authored the ending, state the two accounts the reader is forced to hold, and then set out what the earlier action would have had to contain for the last scene to arrive on its own. A weak answer will call the ending cheap or surprising, which is a complaint about pleasure and not about the plot's causes.

questions.explanation: An explanation of why a device is criticised has to reach the structure rather than the effect. It must name who has authored the ending, since the objection is about authorship of the resolution and not about whether the outcome is welcome. It must state what the reader is able to compare as a result, and that comparison between the plot the play has told and the plot that was announced in the last scene is the part most answers skip, since they settle for a complaint about convenience. And it must say what would have to be true instead, because an explanation that only dismisses leaves the reader with a rule and not with a way of looking at endings. The trap is judging the device by whether the audience enjoyed it, which is a matter of pleasure and not of cause.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What three kinds of chorus do to a play
questions.learningObjective: explain how three different uses of a chorus shape what a reader can learn
questions.stem: In one invented play a chorus enters the action and restrains a character from killing someone. In a second it watches a whole catastrophe and then, afterwards, tells the company what it thinks of it. In a third it reports events it could not have seen, including two that never happened. Explain what each of these three arrangements gives a reader, and what a reader is entitled to assume about a chorus in general.

answer.exemplar: The three arrangements differ in where the chorus stands, and that is what a reader has to establish before anything else. A chorus that acts inside the scene is one of the play's forces, so a reader is entitled to treat what it says as something happening in the world and to ask what its intervention costs the characters around it. A chorus that watches and then comments afterwards has no power over the events and only power over their meaning, so what it offers is a judgment made from outside the interest of anybody in the catastrophe, and a reader has to weigh that judgment rather than accept it. A chorus that reports what it could not have seen has been cut off from the evidence, and its account is now something the reader checks against what the play showed, so the reader is doing a different kind of reading altogether: not asking what the chorus knows but what it is doing with what it has been given. The general entitlement follows from the comparison. A chorus has no automatic authority, because all three of its positions are available to it, and the only safe assumption is that whatever a chorus says, the play has chosen a standpoint from which to say it, and that standpoint has to be worked out from the staging rather than assumed from the convention. The strong explanation will separate the three by their relation to the action, state what each gives a reader, and then draw the general conclusion from the three rather than asserting it in advance. A weak answer will treat the acting chorus as the important one and the other two as defective, which is a ranking the evidence does not support.

questions.explanation: An explanation comparing three arrangements has to be organised on one axis, and the temptation is to treat the three as a scale from best to worst, which is not what they are. They differ in relation to the action, and the axis has to be named explicitly or the comparison turns into three separate descriptions. It must then say what each arrangement gives a reader, and for a chorus that reports what it could not have seen the thing it gives is a check on the text rather than a report about the world. And it must state what generalises, which in this case is a negative entitlement about authority, and the reason it generalises is that all three positions are available to the device. An answer that ends on a claim about which kind of chorus is best has not answered the question asked.
questions.hint: Ask where each chorus stands relative to the action, before asking what any of them says.

questions.topic: What a camera has to be given
questions.learningObjective: explain what an adaptation must supply that the stage did not have to
questions.stem: A play is filmed, and one scene that had run four minutes on stage is nine minutes in the film. The stage version found its long moments in pauses the audience timed together; the film spends its time in close shots, in held sound, and in a slow change of framing. Explain what the two versions do with the same material, and what the film had to decide that the stage never had to.

answer.exemplar: Both versions are asking the audience to experience duration, and they are asking through different materials, which is why the film can be three times as long and be doing the same work. On stage, duration is a matter of what the actors do not do, and the audience times it against itself because it is visibly shared: a pause belongs to the people onstage and to nobody else, and the room supplies the clock. In the film the same four minutes of material has to be built out of what the camera offers, and everything a stage pause gave for free now has to be supplied. The close shot decides which experience is being registered, since it withholds the room and the other characters and makes one face the whole of the event. The held sound supplies time without supplying motion, and it does the particular thing a stage pause does not, which is to be unaffected by what anybody is doing. The slow change of framing supplies a kind of attention a stage cannot offer at all, because a theatre audience looks where it likes while a filmed audience is shown where to look and for how long. What the film had to decide, and what the stage never had to, is the location of the attention. The stage could not control where an audience looked, so its long moments had to be made from what the actors withheld, and a production that wanted a particular reaction had to accept that it might get the opposite one. The film removes that uncertainty and pays for it: it must choose a subject for the duration, and every close shot is a decision about whose experience the minutes belong to. The strong explanation will say what duration is in each version, name the three devices as three different ways of supplying time, and then state the control the camera gains and what the stage gives up. A weak answer will call the film version slower, which is a measurement and not an account of what the extra minutes are made of.

questions.explanation: An explanation comparing two renderings of one passage has to establish what the material is before it compares anything, and here the material is a span of time in which nothing happens and everything is felt. The second duty is to give each version a mechanism rather than a length, because nine minutes is not an explanation and a list of devices is not an explanation either; what is needed is the account of what each device supplies that the other medium supplied differently. The third duty is the one most answers skip, and it is the one the question asks for: an adaptation changes what a production has to decide, and the change is a gain in control purchased with a loss of something the stage had. An answer that ends on a comparison of running times has described the two versions and not the adaptation.
questions.hint: Ask what each device supplies, and then ask what a camera can do with attention that a theatre cannot.
